root_cause.text: Unprivileged users could attach cBPF filters to TCP sockets via SO_ATTACH_FILTER, enabling a side-channel attack to leak sensitive TCP sequence/acknowledgment numbers.
root_cause.evidence: The patch adds a check `if (sk_is_tcp(sk) && !sockopt_ns_capable(..., CAP_NET_ADMIN))` in `sk_setsockopt` for `SO_ATTACH_FILTER`, and the commit message states: "This blocks potential side-channel attack where an unprivileged application attaches a filter to leak TCP sequence/acknowledgment numbers."

candidates.rationale: This case label allows any user to invoke the SO_ATTACH_FILTER operation, which is the entry point for attaching cBPF filters without privilege checks. Without a capability restriction, unprivileged users can reach the filter attachment logic.

Declares the variable that will hold the user-supplied filter program. This is necessary for the subsequent copy from userspace, enabling the injection of arbitrary filter data without prior privilege verification.

Copies the filter program from userspace into kernel memory. Without a check for privileges (e.g., CAP_NET_ADMIN), this allows any user to supply a cBPF filter that can later be used to monitor sensitive data, such as TCP sequence numbers.

Controls the flow to the filter attachment call based on the success of the copy. While not directly vulnerable, it is part of the conditional path that leads to attaching the filter without any privilege check.

Attaches the user-provided cBPF filter to the socket. This is the operation that directly enables the side-channel attack, as the filter can then observe and leak sensitive TCP sequence/acknowledgment numbers during socket traffic.
